---
title: "What is Ownership and Why Does It Exist?"
---

# What is ownership and why does it exist?

Ownership connects a value to responsibility for cleaning up its resources. Rust checks how values move and how they are borrowed, so ordinary safe code can manage resources without manually calling `free`. The same idea applies to more than memory: an owned file handle, for example, can close when its value is dropped.

A useful starting model is that an owned value has one owner at a time; when the owning place is dropped, Rust drops the value. Bindings, fields, and containers can own values. A reference *borrows* access instead of taking ownership. Shared ownership types such as `Rc<T>` provide a different arrangement: several independently owned handles keep one allocation alive. We will distinguish these as the book progresses.

## Scope and cleanup

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("before");
    {
        let task = String::from("desk");
        println!("inside: {task}");
    } // task is dropped here
    println!("after");
}
```

Save as `main.rs` and run `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs -o ownership_demo && ./ownership_demo`. The output is `before`, `inside: desk`, then `after`, each on its own line. The inner braces form a **scope**. The `String` value manages a growable buffer; dropping it releases its owned allocation. An empty string need not allocate, and the exact memory layout is not the ownership rule.

When ownership moves to another binding, the old binding no longer drops the moved value: the new owner is responsible. Assignment can also drop a previously held value before replacing it. Rust normally drops initialized local variables when their scope exits, including during unwinding after a panic; process termination without unwinding, reference cycles, or deliberately leaking a value can prevent destructors from running. Do not rely on `Drop` as a guarantee that every program termination runs cleanup.

## What ownership does and does not promise

The compiler enforces ownership and borrowing rules in safe Rust. Together with correctly implemented standard-library and third-party abstractions, these rules prevent use-after-free and data races in safe code. `unsafe` code has additional obligations: an unsound library can undermine safe callers. Bounds checks, allocation, and other operations can still fail or panic; Rust does not prove that a program is free of logic errors, deadlocks, or all security problems.

Ownership is not a statement that every value is physically stored on the stack, or that a move always copies a heap buffer. The next pages distinguish the **semantic** transfer of ownership from the machine operations the compiler chooses.

## Check yourself

1. What prints after the inner scope in the example? **`after`.**
2. Does borrowing a string give the borrower responsibility for dropping it? **No.** The owner retains that responsibility.
3. Can a Rust program still have a logic bug? **Yes.** Memory safety is not a proof of application correctness.

Reference: [The Rust Programming Language: ownership](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html).
